name: Entropy in Chemistry
tagline: Disorder, spontaneity, and the second law at the molecular scale.
seo_title: Entropy in Chemistry — paper summaries, news & innovations | Chemisters
seo_description: Follow Chemisters Entropy in Chemistry on LinkedIn and Facebook: paper summaries, news and innovations in entropy, the second law, free energy and non-equilibrium chemistry.

definition.lead: Entropy measures how many ways the energy and particles of a system can be arranged, and it decides the direction of every spontaneous change.
definition.body: Ice melts in a warm room, gases mix and perfume spreads because those outcomes can happen in vastly more ways than the alternatives. Combined with enthalpy in the Gibbs energy, entropy predicts which reactions run on their own and where equilibrium settles.

facts.label: Boltzmann's formula, engraved on his tombstone in Vienna
where a perfect crystal reaches its lowest entropy (third law)

branches.name: The second law
branches.summary: The entropy of the universe increases in every spontaneous process.
branches.example: Heat flows from hot to cold, never the reverse on its own.

branches.name: Statistical entropy
branches.summary: Counting the microscopic arrangements behind a macroscopic state.

branches.name: Gibbs energy
branches.summary: Weighing enthalpy against entropy to predict direction.
branches.example: Why some endothermic reactions still run on their own.

branches.name: Mixing & solutions
branches.summary: Mixing increases the number of possible arrangements.
branches.example: Dissolving and osmosis are driven largely by entropy.

branches.name: Third law & absolute entropy
branches.summary: Entropy can be measured from absolute zero.

branches.name: The hydrophobic effect
branches.summary: Water's entropy drives oil and water apart.
branches.example: Proteins fold with their oily parts inside.

branches.name: Information entropy
branches.summary: Shannon's measure of information uses the same mathematics.
branches.example: Data compression and machine learning loss functions.

branches.name: Far-from-equilibrium systems
branches.summary: Systems that create order while increasing total entropy.

timeline.title: Carnot's engine
timeline.text: Sadi Carnot analyses the maximum efficiency of heat engines.
timeline.why: The seed of the second law.

timeline.title: The second law
timeline.text: Rudolf Clausius states that heat does not flow spontaneously from cold to hot.
timeline.why: Gave a direction to natural processes.

timeline.title: Entropy is named
timeline.text: Clausius introduces the word 'entropy', from the Greek for 'transformation'.
timeline.why: A new quantity at the heart of thermodynamics.

timeline.title: The H-theorem
timeline.text: Ludwig Boltzmann derives the approach to equilibrium from molecular collisions.
timeline.why: Linked the second law to the motion of molecules.

timeline.title: Gibbs free energy
timeline.text: Josiah Willard Gibbs begins publishing his theory of heterogeneous equilibrium.
timeline.why: Made entropy usable for chemical reactions.

timeline.title: Counting microstates
timeline.text: Boltzmann connects entropy to the number of molecular arrangements.

timeline.title: The third law
timeline.text: Walther Nernst formulates his heat theorem.
timeline.why: Allowed absolute entropies to be measured.

timeline.title: Onsager's relations
timeline.text: Lars Onsager describes coupled flows near equilibrium.
timeline.why: Founded irreversible thermodynamics; Nobel Prize in 1968.

timeline.title: Information entropy
timeline.text: Claude Shannon defines the entropy of a message.
timeline.why: The same mathematics now runs through computing and AI.

timeline.title: Order from disorder
timeline.text: Nobel Prize to Ilya Prigogine for dissipative structures.
timeline.why: Explained how patterns arise in systems far from equilibrium.

quiz.q: Which of these has the highest entropy?
options: A perfect ice crystal at 0 K
quiz.explain: Gas molecules can be arranged in far more ways than molecules in a liquid or solid.

quiz.q: When a gas expands into a vacuum, its entropy…
quiz.explain: More volume means more possible positions for each molecule.

quiz.q: When can an endothermic process be spontaneous?
quiz.explain: Ice melting above 0 °C absorbs heat but gains enough entropy.

quiz.q: In S = k ln W, W stands for…
According to the third law, a perfect crystal at 0 K has an entropy of…
The hydrophobic effect is driven mostly by…
options: Strong bonds between oil and water
quiz.explain: Water around oily surfaces becomes ordered; grouping the oil together frees that water.

quiz.q: A reaction with ΔH > 0 and ΔS < 0 is…
Can the entropy of a system decrease?
options: Yes, if the entropy of the surroundings increases by more
Only in outer space, far from Earth
Only in liquids, never in solids
quiz.explain: A fridge or a living cell lowers its own entropy while increasing the universe's.

quiz.q: At a melting point, ΔG = 0, so the melting temperature equals…
quiz.explain: Setting ΔH − TΔS = 0 gives T = ΔH/ΔS.

quiz.q: Two ideal gases mix with ΔH ≈ 0. Why do they mix?
quiz.explain: Mixing alone multiplies the number of arrangements.

quiz.q: Ilya Prigogine's 1977 Nobel Prize was for…
options: Proving the third law of thermodynamics
Inventing the first efficient heat engine
quiz.explain: Ordered patterns can form when energy constantly flows through a system.
